description: Our team, based in Hanoi, is a small AI product team. Vietnam has developed a strong agricultural advantage. We want to get involved in data analysis, external factor prediction, and metrics monitoring to help farmers manage their work better with a useful forecasting system. We are open to experts in Software Engineering and Hardware Engineering who want to join us.
summary: We designed a Zalo mini app that gives Vietnamese farmers Trâu (“buffalo”), an assistant that uses NASA data to answer one question: what should I plant next season? Trâu also keeps analyzing conditions and sends farmers daily tips and information about the land they farm. The tool helps farmers see patterns and possibilities, but it doesn’t replace their own judgment or local agricultural expertise.
details:
Trâu ơi (“Hey, Buffalo”) is a Zalo mini app we designed to answer one question for rice farmers in the Mekong Delta: what should I plant on my field next season? We took the Field Shift challenge and narrowed it to saltwater intrusion, which decides that question in the dry season.

A farmer answers two questions: where the field is, and what they planted last year. Trâu then shows the salinity risk for the coming season on a three-level scale and lists the reasons, each one tied to the NASA data layer it came from. It compares three rotations for the same field. Two rice crops is what most farmers do now, so it stays as the baseline. In our example field the risk is high and Trâu suggests rice + shrimp; when the farmer says nobody nearby buys shrimp, it switches to rice + vegetables. Alerts arrive as Zalo messages that name their data source, and the farmer can ask follow-up questions in the same chat. Trâu talks in plain words, so nobody has to read a map. Pests and market prices stay with the farmer, and the app says so.

None of the NASA datasets we use measures salinity directly. Station readings are published as 10-day bulletins, which is too coarse to train a model on. So the model infers next season’s salinity risk from rainfall (GPM IMERG), basin water storage (GRACE-FO), distance to the sea and the history of crop losses. Under it sits a lakehouse on Apache Spark and Delta Lake with 26 tables and more than 1.8 billion rows. We keep every source at its native resolution and join them through the date and a 300 m grid cell. Each table has a description page and a quality report, so anyone can check our work.

The nine years from 2018 to 2026 show no clear trend in rain, heat or soil moisture, and basin water storage has risen about 4 cm per decade since 2002. Two dry seasons stand out. In 2020 and 2024 it rained 88 mm and 68 mm, against a usual 260 mm or so, and the rains came 2 to 4 weeks late. Across the delta, winter-spring rice yields rose from 5.2 t/ha in 1995 to 7.2 t/ha, yet coastal provinces paid for the salty years. In Bến Tre the winter-spring crop fell to 0.05 and 0.04 t/ha in 2016 and 2020, against about 5.1 t/ha in the years around them, and the province almost gave up that season: from 15,000 ha to under 1,000 ha. Trà Vinh lost 38% and 46% of its yield in the same two years and still plants about 62,000 ha every year.

From this we recommend that inland farmers keep planting rice as usual. Coastal farmers should sow winter-spring rice early, from October, to harvest before the salinity peak in February and March, and in salty years move part of their land to rice + shrimp or rice + vegetables. El Niño is strong in 2026 (ONI +2.46), so the coast should treat the 2026-2027 dry season as a salty one.

Fourteen of the 24 data sources suggested by the challenge only cover the United States, so we didn’t use them. Trâu doesn’t forecast yield or give a salinity number. The demo covers one commune, though the model runs for any commune that has data, and the numbers on the prototype screens are still sample values.

We built the data pipeline on Apache Spark and Delta Lake and the interactive prototype in Rive. Zalo is the delivery channel because farmers already use it every day.

After the hackathon we plan to build a map dashboard that lets agricultural engineers see the whole region, check our risk levels against the 10-day bulletins from 28 monitoring stations, ask farmers on Zalo about their water source and buyers, and run the model for more communes.
